duplicate_groups.shared_idea: Possessive its: "it's" before a noun corrected to "its", with the same distractors (its', their/there).
duplicate_groups.evidence: 012 {it's language: its', its, their}; 040 {It's shelves: Its shelves, Their shelves, Its' shelves}; 118 {it's staff: its, their, its'}; 186 {it's brass poles: its', its, there}; 255 {it's cargo: its', their, its}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: Fewer vs. less, using an identical choice set.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 089 {less honey: fewer, lesser, least}; 183 {less knots: fewer, lesser, the least}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: Plural possessive of a regular -s plural, with the same apostrophe-placement choice set.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 079 {sisters' deaths: sister's, sisters, sisters's}; 155 {volunteers records: volunteer's, volunteers's, volunteers'}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: Singular possessive of a -y noun, with the same y/ies apostrophe traps.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 069 {country's: countries', countrys, countries}; 194 {librarys': libraries', library's, libraries}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: A contrast is needed, so the cause or similarity transition becomes 'However'. The choice set is identical.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 002 {Similarly, However, For example, Therefore} ans However; 036 {Therefore, However, Similarly, For example} ans However; 231 {therefore, for example, however, similarly} ans however; 290 {therefore, however, for example, similarly} ans however

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: The original contrast or concession transition is correct (NO CHANGE), against the same distractor trio Therefore / For example / Similarly.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 061 {Yet | Therefore, Similarly, For example}; 103 {However | Therefore, For example, Likewise}; 143 {Nevertheless | Therefore, For example, Similarly}; 242 {Still | Therefore, For example, Similarly}; 269 {Nevertheless | Therefore, For example, Similarly}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: The boundary between two independent clauses is already correct (NO CHANGE), against a comma splice, a fused sentence and a '; and' choice.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 047 {expected. Pigeons | , | none | ; and}; 085 {fluently. I can | , | none | ; and}; 232 {time; the sun | , | none | ; and}; 254 {piece by piece. Dockworkers | , | none | ; and}; 264 {hands. A | , | none | ; and}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon, against a comma splice, a fused sentence and ', and,'. The choice set is identical.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 045 {move, they | move they | move; they | move, and, they}; 190 {weekends; their | weekends, their | weekends their | weekends, and, their}; 236 {it, a | it; a | it a | it, and, a}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon, against a comma splice, a fused sentence and ': and'. The choice set is identical.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 160 {impressed, many | ; many | many | : and many}; 244 {; the | , the | the | : and the}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: An appositive noun phrase after a complete clause takes a comma, not a semicolon or a period. The choice set is identical.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 140 {pianos; a trade: , a / . A / a}; 153 {sightings. A finding: ; a / a / , a}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: No comma between a verb and its that-clause object. The choice set is identical.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 136 {argued, that: argued: that / argued that / argued; that}; 187 {expected, that: expected that / expected: that / expected; that}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: No punctuation between a verb (or participle) and its noun object.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 099 {facing, the sea: facing: / facing the sea / facing;}; 150 {seen, a sea star: seen a sea star / seen; / seen--}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: No comma between a subject and its verb. The choice set is identical.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 205 {Dana Ruiz, helped: no punct / ; / --}; 263 {dabbawalas, collect: no punct / ; / --}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: No colon between a verb and its object.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 226 {needed: a protractor, | ; | , | none}; 273 {held: well over | none | ; | --}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: No comma between a title or descriptor and the name it restricts (poet Fernando Pessoa / librarian Dana Whitfield).
duplicate_groups.evidence: 081 {poet, Fernando Pessoa,: poet, Fernando Pessoa / poet Fernando Pessoa / poet Fernando Pessoa,}; 120 {librarian, Dana Whitfield,: librarian Dana Whitfield, / librarian Dana Whitfield / librarian--Dana Whitfield,}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: An interruption opened with a dash must close with a dash, not a comma.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 119 {packets--tomatoes, beans, and squash, were -> ...squash--were}; 223 {--probably by a falling branch, and -> --...--and}; 267 {The dabbawalas--most of whom ... city, share -> city--share}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: A nonessential relative clause between the subject and the main verb is missing its closing comma.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 011 {Rosa, who has guided rafting trips for twenty years [no comma] kept -> ...years,}; 288 {The firms' reply, which arrived some weeks later [no comma] was -> later, was}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: A nonessential participial phrase between the subject and the verb, correctly set off by paired commas (NO CHANGE), against choices that drop a comma or use a semicolon.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 001 {Their logbooks, now stored in a state archive, record: drop 1st comma / drop 2nd comma / semicolon}; 209 {the station, running on a generator, became: drop closing comma / semicolon / , and became}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: An unnecessary comma splits a restrictive clause from its introducer (that, / the way, / where,). The fix is to remove it, and the distractors move the comma later in the clause.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 082 {that, I eventually translated as | remove | that I, eventually | translated, as}; 083 {the way, my grandmother saw | remove | the way: | grandmother, saw}; 102 {where, a listener | where; | where a listener, | remove}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: The relative pronoun is the subject of a clause about a person, so the answer is 'who'. 148 and 207 use the identical choice set.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 148 {which teaches: whom, whose, who}; 207 {whom had planned: which, whose, who}; 256 {whom organized: which organized, who organized, that he organized}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: 'Whoever' is the subject of its own clause, so 'whomever' and 'whom' are wrong.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 107 {by whomever stands: whoever, whom, whichever}; 117 {whoever buys [NO CHANGE]: whomever, whom, who's}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: In a compound object, 'X and I' should be 'X and me'. The choice set is identical.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 214 {my partner and I: myself, me, mine}; 241 {Delia and I: myself, mine, me}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: An adjective modifies a verb and must become an -ly adverb, with comparative and noun-form distractors.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 015 {quick: quicker, more quick, quickly}; 217 {careful: carefully, more careful, with care and carefully}; 270 {consistent: consistence, more consistent, consistently}; 296 {knowledgeable: more knowledgeable, knowledgeably, knowledge}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: The noun 'affect' is corrected to 'effect'.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 145 {a strong affect on: affection, effect, effecting}; 222 {The affect of the project: affects, effect, affected}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: Faulty comparison of a thing with a place or source, fixed by restating the noun ('honey from the countryside' / 'tomatoes from commercial packets').
duplicate_groups.evidence: 095 {different from the countryside: the countryside does / honey from the countryside / in the countryside}; 122 {earlier than commercial packets: commercial packets do / that of the commercial seed packets / tomatoes from commercial packets}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: 'Then' is corrected to 'than' after a comparative.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 114 {harder then: harder than / more harder than / hardest than}; 216 {more willing ... then: when / as / than}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: 'Could of' is corrected to a correct modal verb form.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 197 {could of toppled: could topple / could have toppling / can toppled}; 247 {could not of handled: could not handled / could not handling / could not handle}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: An irregular verb given a regular -ed past tense (lended, costed) is corrected to its irregular form.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 087 {lended: had lended, lent, lends}; 167 {costed: cost, has cost, costing}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: 'Each of' + plural noun takes a singular verb.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 059 {Each of these numbers are recorded -> is}; 179 {Each of the hundreds of books ... were -> was}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: In a series of three past-tense verbs, the third is wrongly an -ing form, with the same distractor set (-ing / past / had + past).
duplicate_groups.evidence: 049 {soaked..., and scrubbing}; 172 {replaced, filled, and repainting: repainted, had repainted, was repainting}; 284 {opened, reached, and wiping: wiped, had wiped, wipes}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: In a series of past-tense verbs, the third item wrongly adds a subject pronoun ('and he read', 'and then she glued', 'and it also flattened').
duplicate_groups.evidence: 068 {opened its louvered door, and he read -> and read}; 178 {and then she glued: gluing, glued, had glued}; 280 {and it also flattened: flattening, flattened, had flattened}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: A present-tense verb inside a past-tense narrative is corrected to simple past, against will-, are -ing and has- forms.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 201 {monitor: will monitor, monitored, are monitoring}; 215 {visit: will visit, are visiting, visited}; 240 {asks: has asked, asked, will ask}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: Present perfect used for an action before another past time is corrected to past perfect.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 152 {has tripled: triples, had tripled, will triple}; 275 {has leaked: leaks, would leak, had leaked}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: A singular head noun followed by 'of' + plural takes a singular verb (the variety ... has / the measure ... remains).
duplicate_groups.evidence: 126 {have: were, has, having}; 271 {remain: remains, are remaining, have remained}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: A plural subject with 'was' is corrected to 'were'. The choice set is identical.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 023 {most of them was: has been, were, is}; 100 {they was: were, is, has been}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: The same idiom: 'comply to' is corrected to 'comply with'.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 091 {comply to: by, on, with}; 230 {comply to: for, at, with}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: A vague or informal phrase is replaced by the one concrete, specific choice, while the other choices stay vague or wordy. The reasoning and choice pattern are the same.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 030 {got kind of messed up: experienced problems / peeled and faded / were not so good}; 144 {certain useful items: things of various kinds / ...every possible sort / ivory keys, brass pedals, and tuning pins}; 225 {was nice about it and helped us out a lot: lent us a small vise and sold us a bronze rod at cost / ...}; 238 {in various different kinds of conditions: some smiling, some grimacing, and some walking / ...}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: A colon introduces an independent clause that explains the clause before it, against a comma, no punctuation and a conjunction distractor. The choice set is the same.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 071 {consistent, in | in | : in | , and, in}; 124 {rule, seeds | : seeds | seeds | ; and seeds}; 252 {: it | , it | it | ; and it}

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: Essay-goal item where the goal is instructional (how to save seeds / how to start a beehive) but the essay profiles one organization. The answer is 'No, because it profiles X rather than giving instructions', and both have a 'No, because it argues X fails/is dangerous' distractor.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 044 D 'No, because it mainly recounts how one library's seed program grew' / C 'argues that most seed libraries fail'; 098 D 'No, because it profiles one hotel's rooftop hives rather than giving instructions' / C 'argues that keeping bees in cities is too dangerous'

duplicate_groups.shared_idea: Essay-goal item where the goal is 'how an ordinary routine/observation led to something valuable'. The answer is Yes in both, with the same distractors: technical-detail Yes, 'focuses mainly on' side topic No, and an irrelevant-fact No.
duplicate_groups.evidence: 078 goal 'one volunteer's ordinary routine produced something of scientific value' A Yes / B 'explains in detail how thermometers...are built'; 292 goal 'how an ordinary observation led to a useful invention' A Yes / B 'explains how electric wipers replaced...'

close_but_kept.why_kept: Both correct 'their' to 'its' with {it's, its, its'}, but the antecedents differ (collective noun 'club' vs. 'each of the keys'), so they are different agreement triggers.
Both are singular possessives, but 287 (firms' -> firm's) has no -y/-ies trap and uses a different choice set.
The choice set {for, of, to, about} is identical, but the idioms differ ('in search of' vs. 'responsible for') and so does the direction (fix vs. NO CHANGE).

Concession or theory-practice transitions that are correct as written. The distractor wording differs from group 61 and from each other (As a result / In other words / For instance), as do the specific relations (admission, theory vs. practice, expectation).
Both have 'For this reason,' correct as NO CHANGE, but two of the three distractors differ. Watch this one if another cause/effect item with the same answer is added.
Same construction (subject, who-clause, verb), but 058 is NO CHANGE and has a broader distractor set. It is borderline, and the 011/288 group already covers the missing-closing-comma error.
Past perfect, but 026 is correct as written with a 'since' cue and has different distractors.
Present perfect for a span reaching the present, but the cues differ: 129 relies on context, 233 has an explicit 'For the past three years', and 233 is NO CHANGE.
Agreement across 'of' + plural, but 139 is correct as written with different distractors.
Plural subject with a singular verb, but 291 is a present-tense -s verb ('few drivers knows') with a different choice set.
Both are inverted-sentence agreement, but 013 also tests lie/lay and is NO CHANGE, and the choice sets differ.
Both are hypothetical conditionals, but the errors differ (was -> were subjunctive vs. will return -> returned).
Both put a comma before a nonessential which-clause, but 218 tests matching a mid-sentence opener to its later closing comma, while 204's clause is at the end of the sentence.
Both put a comma before 'and' in a compound sentence, but 258 is a garden-path missing comma ('cranes and shipping companies') and 163 is NO CHANGE, with different choice sets.

Each is a fragment created by a period before a dependent element, but the elements differ (relative clause, participial phrase, prepositional phrase, subordinate clause, introductory phrase). These are different constructions, like the comma-splice example in the rule.

Sentence-boundary templates were kept as separate groups by exact choice pattern (period/'; and', semicolon/', and,', semicolon/': and'). 106 and 147 have unique fourth choices. A reviewer could reasonably merge groups 47, 45 and 160 into one.
Doubled-synonym redundancy in the same passage (P016: 'chose and selected', 'ceaselessly, and tirelessly'). The word class and phrases differ, but consider revising one for variety.
Both are time-of-day redundancy ('in the evening at night', 'at night when it is dark'), but the phrases and choice sets differ.
Both are 'No' essay-goal items (a technology goal vs. an essay about human craft or a human system), but the reasoning differs: 272 turns on the essay's point that no new technology is used.

Both are 'Yes' essay-goal items about one person's contribution, but the goals differ (solving a community problem vs. ordinary routine yielding scientific value). Note that 078, 088, 109, 166, 213 and 292 all use the same A-Yes / B-'explains in detail' / C-'focuses mainly on' / D template. Vary the template in future items.

Conclusion items: one per passage, each tied to its own essay's opening. The stem is formulaic but each item depends on its passage, so none are duplicates. Five of them (010, 021, 042, 053, 076) are correct as NO CHANGE.
Sentence-order and placement items share ACT's fixed choice formats, but the reasoning in each depends on its own passage.
Both are object-case pronouns, but the constructions differ (compound object vs. object of 'between').

passage_repeats.why: Same specific subject and arc. A public library starts a seed-lending program in 2019 and doubts anyone will use it. Patrons borrow in spring and return saved seeds in fall, demand grows to hundreds of packets, and squash cross-pollination spoils returned seeds, so staff add a labeling rule. Both share the title 'The Seed Library'. They also produce duplicate items (040 and 118 both test 'it's' + noun). Strongest repeat: rewrite or replace P012.

Same argument. Decades of routine handwritten weather records (lighthouse keepers / a volunteer observer) become valuable to climate scientists because they form an unbroken record from one place, and researchers use them to show local warming. The keepers or observer never imagined that use.

Same story arc. A beloved town landmark (courthouse clock / carousel) stops working for over a decade. A retired craftsperson (factory machinist / shop teacher) volunteers and restores it by hand, rebuilding worn parts one at a time, and a crowd gathers or lines up when it runs again. This is a moderate repeat: the objects differ but the narrative and argument are the same.

notes: Bank has 302 questions and 30 passages. CLD-ACT-E-000170 is already retired (hold-defect) and was skipped, leaving 301 live items. Method: grouped live items by normalized subskill and by normalized choice set (NO CHANGE ignored), then read each item's underlined construction in passage context. The rule applied: same specific rule tested the same way with an essentially identical choice set, or the same error type in the same construction. Within each group the lowest id is kept. No later item was clearly better, except that 107 (whomever after 'by') is the richer whoever item and is also the earlier one. Results: 40 groups and 63 proposed retirements. The largest clusters are transitions with the stock distractor trio Therefore / For example / Similarly, sentence-boundary items with a stock comma-splice / fused / '; and' set, and its/it's. These are template-level duplicates: they differ only in sentence content. If the bank owner wants to keep transition and boundary coverage, the retired items could be rewritten with fresh distractor sets instead of dropped. Other findings: (1) passage-title metadata defect: P007, P008, P009, P010 and P011 are all titled 'Mapping the Dark' (P006's title), though their topics are a weather observer, a grandmother's letters, rooftop bees, sound mirrors and a night market; (2) thematic adjacency, not flagged as a repeat: P003 (sign painter, hand vs. vinyl machine) and P018 (bookbinder who refuses 'the shortcut' machine) both value handcraft over machines but have different subjects and arcs; P023 (club fixes a sundial) is another fix-the-broken-landmark story, related to P005/P017. Passage repeats are reported separately and do not themselves retire items.

decision.rule: Retired (a) every item on the three essays that repeat an earlier essay's story or argument (P012, P007, P017) and (b) later items whose four choices are word-for-word the same context-free set as an earlier item testing the same fix (255, 183, 241, 100; 186 also falls under P017). Kept the remaining groups: they test one rule on different sentences with sentence-specific choices, so solving each requires reading its own sentence; retiring them would remove most rule coverage from an ACT English bank, which by design needs several items per rule. Kept 040 (different choice form). Going forward: vary distractor sets (avoid the stock 'Therefore / For example / Similarly' trio and repeated token sets) and check new essays against every existing essay's topic and argument.
